screeningSummary: Daughter asks to tell her late mother's 1974 sighting - laughed out of the family, it lived only in a pencil diary
arcNotes: Emotional question arc. Vern treats it as the show's core purpose, shares the '74 decade context (laughter at home, silence elsewhere), reframes the diary as a message to the daughter, and has her tell it on air in full - name, orchard, year. Tender close

lines.text: My mom passed in January. In 1974, she saw something over our orchard - a light that stopped and watched her, and then left. She told her family once. They laughed. She never said the word again - not once in fifty years. I found her journal. Three pages, in pencil. Can I - I know this isn't a sighting. Can I tell it for her?

lines.text: Not up - toward. Your mother wrote like a witness, because she was one. And I'll tell you what my files say about 1974, because she wasn't alone in it: that was a big year for lights, and a bad year for telling. That was the decade when a woman who saw something got two reactions - laughter at home and silence everywhere else. The ones who kept journals did what the decade forced on them: they told the paper instead, and paper outlives laughter. Fifty years later, here you are, reading her. That's not luck - that's her knowing her family would fail her, and deciding the pencil wouldn't. She wasn't writing to be believed in 1974. She was writing to be believed by you.
